newsitem.title: USA: Tough US, EU meat talks to resume, hurdles remain.
newsitem.headline: Tough US, EU meat talks to resume, hurdles remain.

text.p: Difficult talks to resolve a bitter trade dispute between the United States and the European Union over meat imports were set to resume Wednesday, but industry officials said Tuesday that key obstacles still remain toward reaching an agreement.
"There are some key points on the poultry side that still need to be worked out," said Stewart Proctor, president of the National Turkey Federation.
"I don't think there's much flexibility left," said Len Condon of the American Meat Institute.

U.S. and EU officials are trying to reach an agreement in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks that would enable each side to purchase meat and poultry products from the other, even if their inspection systems differ.

Failure to reach agreement has already halted U.S. poultry exports to Europe -- disrupting a market of some $50 million -- and threatens to block around $300 million of European meat products to the United States by the end of the month.
Washington has threatened to take more than 100 European meat and poultry packing plants off its list of approved exporters on April 30 if the dispute is not settled.
Washington last week extended an earlier deadline of April 15, but Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman on Monday ruled out another delay.
"I will say there will be no more extensions," Glickman told the National Association of Agricultural Journalists.

Poultry issues have remained the key sticking points in the talks. While progress has reportedly been made in several other non-poultry areas, U.S. and EU officials still are in disagreement over how the U.S. poultry industry decontaminates carcasses with a chlorine solution.

The European Union has offered an interim plan that would allow U.S. poultry processors to use lactic acid and TSP as decontaminants, but not chlorine. The U.S. poultry industry contends that these methods are costly and not as effective as chlorine, and that the EU is using the chlorine issue as a way to keep U.S. poultry out of the European market.

"This whole discussion of chlorine is a ruse ... The Europeans are trying to accomplish a decades-long goal of erecting non-tarriff trade barriers and blocking U.S. exports to their markets," said Proctor of the Turkey Federation.
Whether the United States would accept an agreement on everything except poultry was unclear.

Observers noted that the U.S. poultry industry is a powerful political force, and also pointed out that it might endanger the huge Russian market for U.S. poultry if the issue with Europe is not settled.
"The poultry industry is worried about the impact on the Russian market ... the Russians might do the same thing," said an industry official.

Loss of the Russian market would be a devastating blow to the U.S. industry. In recent years, Russia has become the biggest foreign customer for U.S. poultry parts, buying well over $500 million worth last year.
